name: QUANTUM OF SAL- BURGER (comes with salsa and chipotle)

recipe.history:
Salsa — the word simply means sauce in Spanish — is one of the oldest condiment traditions in the Americas, predating European contact by thousands of years. The Aztecs, Mayans, and other Mesoamerican civilizations ground tomatoes, chili peppers, squash seeds, and various aromatics into preparations that Spanish colonizers documented in the sixteenth century as both food and medicine. The tomato itself, native to western South America and cultivated in Mexico, was regarded with deep suspicion by early European settlers who believed it was poisonous — a conviction that persisted in parts of Europe well into the eighteenth century. Chipotle — from the Nahuatl word chilpoctli, meaning smoked chili — is a jalapeño pepper that has been smoke-dried over wood, a preservation and flavor technique developed by the indigenous people of Mexico's high-altitude regions where the cooler climate made fresh pepper preservation difficult. Together, tomato-based salsa and smoky chipotle represent the deep, pre-colonial culinary intelligence of Mesoamerica, a flavor tradition that has been feeding people with extraordinary sophistication for thousands of years.

Salsa overtook ketchup as America's best-selling condiment in the early 1990s, a statistic that made headlines and announced the definitive demographic and culinary shift underway in American food culture. Mexican and Mexican-American cuisine had long been woven into the food of the American Southwest and California, but the national mainstreaming of salsa represented something broader — an acknowledgment that the tomato-chili sauce tradition of Mesoamerica was more complex, more interesting, and more versatile than the sweet vinegar-tomato reduction that had dominated American tables since the nineteenth century. Chipotle peppers in adobo sauce — canned, accessible, and shelf-stable — became one of the most transformative pantry items in American home cooking through the 1990s and 2000s. On a burger, chipotle salsa brings smoke, heat, acidity, and the ghost of an ancient culinary tradition that makes a simple beef patty taste like something larger and more intentional.

I made my first batch of chipotle salsa during a summer in New Mexico that I spent mostly eating breakfast burritos and reading novels on a borrowed porch. A neighbor brought over tomatoes from her garden and a can of chipotles in adobo she said she bought at the grocery store but I was certain she conjured it from pure generosity. I roasted the tomatoes in the oven until they collapsed and blackened at the edges, blended them with two chipotle peppers and a splash of their adobo sauce, added salt and lime juice, and tasted something that stopped me completely. The smokiness was architectural — it gave the sauce a depth that felt ancient, like it had been worked out over generations rather than invented on a Tuesday afternoon. I put it on everything for the rest of that summer, and eventually I put it on a burger and understood that some condiments are not just flavoring agents but small history lessons.

The medium-rare burger — cooked to the internal temperature window of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — is the only vessel worthy of a chipotle salsa this complex. The reason is simple: at medium rare, the beef is still a juicy, fat-rich, deeply flavored thing that can stand in conversation with the smoke and acidity of the chipotle. The tomato's brightness, the pepper's smoky heat, the adobo sauce's sweetness — they need a patty that has something to say back. An overcooked, dry burger patty cannot hold this conversation; it just absorbs the salsa like a sponge and disappears. Medium rare is the temperature of intention, the proof that you took this burger seriously from the first choice of beef through the last touch of the lid.
ingredients: 1 egg + 1 tbsp water for egg wash
680g ground beef (80/20 chuck blend), freshly ground
2 to 3 chipotle peppers in adobo sauce
1 tbsp adobo sauce from the can
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, sugar, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy.
2. Add egg and softened butter. Mix briefly. Add bread flour and salt. Knead with dough hook on medium speed for 8 minutes until smooth.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
4. Divide into 4 portions (~150g each), shape into tight rounds, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash and sprinkle sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.

6. Make the chipotle salsa: Preheat broiler to high. Place tomato halves cut-side up, onion pieces, and unpeeled garlic cloves on a foil-lined baking sheet. Broil 10 to 12 minutes until tomatoes are charred and collapsing and garlic is soft. Peel garlic. Blend tomatoes, onion, roasted garlic, chipotle peppers, adobo sauce, lime juice, cilantro, salt, and sugar in a blender until desired consistency (chunky or smooth). Taste and adjust seasoning. Cool to room temperature.
7. Make the chipotle mayo: Stir together mayonnaise, minced chipotle, adobo sauce, lime juice, and salt. Refrigerate until needed.

8. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (170g each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a center dimple. Season both sides with salt, pepper, cumin, and smoked paprika immediately before cooking.
9. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil.
10. Place patties in the pan. Cook 2 minutes undisturbed. Flip once. Top each patty with a slice of pepper jack cheese immediately.
11. Cook 1.5 to 2 minutes more, tenting with foil, until an instant-read thermometer reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
12. Toast the buns: Butter cut sides and toast face-down in a skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.
13. Assemble: Spread chipotle mayo on both cut faces of each bun.
14. Layer shredded lettuce on the bottom bun, then avocado slices and red onion rings.
15. Place the medium-rare pepper jack patty on top. Spoon 2 to 3 tablespoons of chipotle salsa generously over the patty.
16. Cap with the top bun. Serve with lime wedges and extra salsa on the side.
